question: What is the maximum fee for a traditional Florida notarial act?

options.why: Correct. §117.05(2) caps most traditional notarial acts at $10 each.
Wrong. $15 is California's per-signature fee.
Wrong. $2 is New York's fee.
Wrong. $25 is Florida's cap for online notarizations, not traditional acts.

explanation: Florida notaries may charge up to $10 for each notarial act.

refs.title: Governor's Reference Manual for Notaries: Notary Public Fees (p. 11)

question: What is the maximum fee for an online notarization in Florida?

options.why: Correct. §117.275 allows up to $25 per online notarization.
Wrong. $10 is the traditional-act cap.
Wrong. $50 is twice the online cap.
Wrong. $5 understates the online fee.

explanation: Online notarizations may be charged up to $25.

question: For which act may a Florida notary NOT charge a fee?

options.why: Correct. §117.05(2) bars a fee for witnessing a vote-by-mail (absentee) ballot.
Wrong. Deed acknowledgments may be charged up to $10.
Wrong. Affidavits may be charged up to $10.
Wrong. Attested photocopies may be charged up to $10.

explanation: No fee may be charged for witnessing a vote-by-mail ballot.

refs.title: Governor's Reference Manual for Notaries: Notary Public Fees (p. 11)

question: Two people sign and acknowledge one deed. Florida charges per notarial act. What is the maximum?

options.why: Correct. Each signer's acknowledgment is a separate notarial act, so two acts × $10 = $20.
Wrong. Two signers' acknowledgments are two acts.
Wrong. Florida has no $1 additional-signature rate; that's Texas.
Wrong. $30 would be three acts.

explanation: Each acknowledgment is a notarial act charged up to $10.

question: What fee may be charged for an attested photocopy?

options.why: Correct. Attesting a photocopy is a notarial act, capped at $10 under §117.05(2).
Wrong. $25 is the online notarization fee, not the photocopy fee.
Wrong. A fee of up to $10 is allowed.
Wrong. Florida doesn't charge per page for attested photocopies.

explanation: Attesting a photocopy is a notarial act with a $10 maximum.

question: What fee may a Florida notary charge for solemnizing a marriage?

options.text: The fee set by statute for clerks of court for performing marriage ceremonies
options.why: Correct. §117.045 lets a notary charge the fee clerks of court may charge for performing a marriage ceremony.
Wrong. The fee is limited by statute; it isn't open-ended.
Wrong. Marriages aren't billed at the general $10 rate.
Wrong. A fee is allowed for solemnizing a marriage.

explanation: A notary may charge the same fee clerks of court charge for marriage ceremonies.

refs.title: Governor's Reference Manual for Notaries: Solemnizing Marriages (p. 17)

options.why: Correct. Fees are ceilings; a notary may charge less or nothing.
Wrong. They are maximums.
Wrong. Charging more is an overcharge, so they aren't minimums.
Wrong. Every listed fee is a maximum.

question: A notary charges $20 for one acknowledgment. What is true?

options.text: It is an overcharge and grounds for suspension
options.why: Correct. Charging over the $10 cap violates §117.05(2) and is grounds for suspension.
Wrong. A signer's consent can't authorize an illegal fee.
Wrong. Document length doesn't change the cap.
Wrong. There's no after-hours rate.

question: Does Florida law require a non-attorney notary's advertising in a language other than English to list the notary's fees?

options.text: No; it requires only the 'not an attorney' notice, in English and the language of the ad
options.why: Correct. §117.05(10) requires a conspicuous notice stating "I am not an attorney licensed to practice law in the State of Florida, and I may not give legal advice or accept fees for legal advice"; it does not require a fee schedule.

options.text: Yes, the full fee schedule must be posted
options.why: Wrong. Unlike Texas and California, Florida's §117.05(10) requires only the 'not an attorney' notice, not the fees.

options.text: Yes, but only the $10 maximum fee
options.why: Wrong. No statement of fees is required; the notice is the requirement.

options.text: No; non-English advertising needs no notice at all
options.why: Wrong. The 'not an attorney' notice is mandatory, in English and the language of the ad.

explanation: A non-attorney notary who advertises in another language must include, in English and that language, the notice "I am not an attorney licensed to practice law in the State of Florida, and I may not give legal advice or accept fees for legal advice" (§117.05(10)). Florida does not require the ad to list fees.

question: An online notary takes one online acknowledgment. What is the maximum fee?

options.why: Correct. Florida allows up to $25 for an online notarization.
Wrong. Florida doesn't stack the act fee on top of the online fee; $35 is the Texas total.
Wrong. $10 is the traditional-act cap.
Wrong. $50 is double the online cap.

explanation: Florida allows up to $25 for an online notarization.

question: May a Florida notary charge a separate travel fee?

options.text: Yes, if the signer agrees in advance; it isn't a notarial fee
options.why: Correct. Travel is a separate service; the notary may charge for it if the signer agrees in advance.
Wrong. Travel fees are generally allowed by agreement.
Wrong. Travel isn't capped at the $10 notarial fee.
Wrong. Travel fees aren't limited to marriages.

explanation: Travel fees may be charged if agreed in advance and kept separate from the notarial fee.

question: Must a Florida notary charge a fee?

options.why: Correct. Fees are optional maximums.
Wrong. A notary may waive the fee.
Wrong. The day of the week is irrelevant.
Wrong. Fees don't depend on whether the notary knows the customer.

question: A notary administers an oath for one affidavit and attests one photocopy for the same customer. What is the maximum total?

options.why: Correct. Two separate acts at up to $10 each = $20.
Wrong. Two acts were performed.
Wrong. $25 is the online notarization fee.
Wrong. $30 would be three acts.

explanation: Each act is up to $10: $20 total.

question: Who sets Florida's maximum notary fees?

options.why: Correct. The Legislature sets maximum fees in chapter 117.
Wrong. Notaries can't exceed the statutory caps.
Wrong. County clerks don't set notary fees.
Wrong. Bonding agencies don't set notary fees.

explanation: Maximum fees are set by statute.
